title: A Two-Year-Old Indian Restaurant in Small-Town Michigan Is Competing for a World Culinary Award
excerpt: KT's Rasoi in St. Joseph has been nominated for North America's Best Indian Cuisine Restaurant at the 7th annual World Culinary Awards, going up against established names across the continent.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • KT's Rasoi in St. Joseph, Michigan, is nominated for North America's Best Indian Cuisine.
  • The restaurant opened two years ago, focusing on authentic Indian dishes.
  • Voting for the World Culinary Awards is open until August 14.
  • The nomination highlights the rise of quality Indian cuisine in smaller U.S. towns.
  • KT's Rasoi's biryani and dosas showcase commitment to culinary authenticity.
A Small Town's Big Culinary Dream
›Nominated for North America's Best Indian Cuisine
›Located in St. Joseph, Michigan, population ~8,000
›Opened two years ago with a focus on authenticity
›Competing against established names from major cities
World Culinary Awards
Most stories about Indian restaurants making international headlines involve big-city establishments — Michelin-starred tasting rooms in Manhattan, celebrated fine-dining spots in San Francisco and Chicago. But the latest Indian restaurant to earn a global nomination is in St. Joseph, Michigan, a lakeside town of about 8,000 people best known for its beaches and lighthouses. KT's Rasoi Indian Cuisine, tucked away at 4075 Hollywood Road, has been officially nominated for North America's Best Indian Cuisine Restaurant at the 7th annual World Culinary Awards — the hospitality industry's equivalent of the Oscars, where the winner is decided entirely by public vote. ## From a Handful of Recipes to a Global Stage The restaurant opened just two years ago with what its team describes as "a handful of our favorite recipes" — authentic Hyderabadi Chicken Dum Biryani, crispy dosas, refreshing mango lassi and a few signature dishes. The focus was straightforward: serve truly authentic Indian food to the local community. "When we opened our doors just two years ago, we had one simple goal: to serve truly authentic Indian food to our amazing community," the KT's Rasoi team shared on social media. "To be recognised on a global stage alongside some of the finest restaurants in North America is a dream come true." That dream is now very much alive. The World Culinary Awards, now in its seventh year, evaluates restaurants across categories spanning every continent. A nomination in the North America category puts KT's Rasoi shoulder to shoulder with established names from New York, Los Angeles, Toronto and beyond. ## The Power of Authenticity in Unexpected Places KT's Rasoi's nomination reflects a broader trend in the Indian diaspora food landscape: the decentralisation of quality Indian dining. While cities with large South Asian populations — Edison and Jersey City in New Jersey, Fremont in California, Jackson Heights in Queens — have long had excellent Indian restaurants, the expansion of authentic Indian cuisine into smaller American cities and towns is a relatively new phenomenon. In Columbus, Ohio, the Kondhare family is opening Bombay House this month with a pan-India menu spanning Mumbai street food to South Indian specialties. In Longmont, Colorado, a Michelin-recognised chef from Beverly Hills is setting up a 1,300-square-foot Indian kitchen. In Austin, Texas, Rock 'N' Grill has won the Consumer Choice Award for Indian dining three years running. The common thread? Indian families and chefs who refuse to water down their food for perceived American palates. ## Hyderabadi Biryani in Michigan
Voting Dynamics for Culinary Recognition
›Voting open until August 14
›Votes from industry professionals count double
›Supports the global Indian diaspora community
›Validates authenticity over location in culinary prestige
World Culinary Awards
KT's Rasoi's signature Hyderabadi Chicken Dum Biryani is a case in point. Traditional dum biryani — slow-cooked in a sealed pot, the rice layered with marinated meat and aromatic spices — is one of India's most technically demanding dishes. Many Indian restaurants outside major metros simplify the process. KT's Rasoi does not. The restaurant's dosas — thin, crispy crepes made from a fermented rice and lentil batter — are another indicator of its commitment to authenticity. Good dosa-making requires precise batter fermentation, the right griddle temperature and a cook's practiced hand. These are not shortcuts you can take in a commercial kitchen without someone who learned the craft in India. ## What Voting Means for the Diaspora The World Culinary Awards winner is chosen entirely by public vote, with voting open until August 14. In a twist that speaks to the global nature of the Indian diaspora, voters from the culinary, travel or hospitality industries get their ballots counted double — a provision that could help rally support from the extensive network of Indian hospitality professionals across North America. For the NRI community, the nomination is bigger than one restaurant. It validates the idea that authentic Indian food does not need a big-city postcode or a Michelin inspector's blessing to earn global respect. Sometimes it just needs a family with a few great recipes and the conviction to cook them right. ## What's Next Voting closes on August 14, and the winners will be announced at a ceremony later this year. Win or lose, KT's Rasoi has already accomplished something remarkable: putting St. Joseph, Michigan on the global Indian food map — one plate of biryani at a time.
